evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.8.6: īnfrā etiam natāre concessum
Cic. Tusc. 5.100: nōn sōlum in praesentiā, sed etiam posterō diē
terms.comment: Adds a further fact or person, before or after the word: nōn sōlum (modo) … sed etiam, not only … but also. In a question, Etiamne …?: etiamne hoc negābis? (Plaut. Am. 2.2.128, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Ov. Rem. 104: crās quoque fīet idem
Liv. 1.9.3: urbēs quoque, ut cētera, ex īnfimō nāscī
terms.comment: Always straight after the word it marks: mē quoque, me too (Hor. C. 1.16.22, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Stich. 2.1.44: Salvus sīs. — Et tū salvē. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In greetings and answers: et tū, you too; et ego, so did I (Cic. Sen. 26). In narrative, Lewis & Short: frequent in Livy, rare in Cicero.

evidence: Quint. 1.11.5: cum C ac similiter G nōn ēvaluērunt
terms.comment: The adverb of similis (see similar): alike, in a like manner.

phrases.latin: Valē. — Et tū; numquid vīs aliud?
phrases.english: Goodbye. — You too. Is there anything else you want?
we keep saying, ‘it will be the same tomorrow too’

phrases.latin: et ego fēcī quī litterās Graecās senex didicī
phrases.english: so did I, who learned Greek as an old man
